method: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis' (last updated July 2019). Every claim is a paraphrase backed by anchors (scripts/anchor.py): verify.py --source re-finds each anchored span in a fresh copy of the source, checks the claim's numbers against it and rejects copying. LICENCE: © The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; Terms clause 5.2, personal use only; paraphrased and hash-anchored (read at RCH Terms and Conditions, clause 5.2 (rch.org.au)). The source's words are NOT reproduced here. Edition 2.0 rebuilds the Wave 1 hand-written edition (verbatim quotes) as paraphrase against the page fetched 2026-09-24. Every clinical claim of edition 1.0 is carried over; the last-updated claim now sits in the source date and a banner. The page marks red flags by colour, which text extraction loses, so no red-flag list is given.

claims.claim: **Becoming dry at night is part of normal development, and the age it happens varies widely.** Bedwetting runs strongly in families.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Day control usually comes by 4 years; night control comes later and is not expected before 5-7 years.** Almost 1 in 3 four-year-olds still wet the bed, dropping to around 1 in 10 at 6 years.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Bedwetting is common and rarely leaves lasting harm.** Because so many children grow out of it, treatment usually waits until age 6.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Possible mechanisms:** producing a lot of urine overnight (nocturnal polyuria), an overactive detrusor, and being hard to rouse (a raised arousal threshold).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The trigger for treatment is social:** for most children bedwetting only becomes a problem when it gets in the way of friendships (sleepovers, school camps). If wetting is occasional or not upsetting the child or parents, no treatment is needed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Most children who wet have no significant physical or emotional cause,** yet many feel ashamed or embarrassed and lose self-esteem, more so as they get older.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Monosymptomatic enuresis (MSE):** night wetting with no other lower urinary tract symptom and no history of bladder dysfunction.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Daytime lower urinary tract symptoms change the approach;** if they are the main problem, consider treating them before the bedwetting.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Voiding habits are the core of the history.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Recent onset (the last few days or weeks)?** Ask whether this could be how a systemic illness is presenting.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Was the child dry at night, unaided, for 6 months before?** Secondary enuresis that persists without explanation despite good management should go to a specialist.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Ask about daytime symptoms:** frequency, urgency, polyuria, dysuria or recurrent UTI, a weak stream or straining, and leakage.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Also ask about** bowels (constipation, soiling); sleep set-up and routine (own bed or room, snoring, broken sleep); and comorbid conditions — diabetes mellitus, sleep apnoea, or developmental or behavioural problems.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Social history:** how able and motivated the family is to take on treatment, and any social difficulty that makes the child or family vulnerable.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Examine:** height, weight and BP (poor growth, weight loss, hypertension); abdomen for a distended bladder or faecal mass; ⚠️ lower back and spine for occult spinal dysraphism or tethered cord (a deviated or asymmetric gluteal cleft); lower limb neurology.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Primary enuresis needs no dipstick urinalysis** unless red flags are present, and imaging or blood tests are not routine.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat any constipation properly first, then tackle the wetting.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Drink and void regularly through the day** (for example at school breaks) and again right before bed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Do not restrict fluids, but cut out caffeinated drinks in the evening.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Explain** how the bladder normally works and why bedwetting happens, including that it runs in families; tell them it is common among the child's peers and nothing to be embarrassed about.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Behavioural treatment needs a motivated parent and a motivated child** before it starts.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Over 6 years, an alarm is the most effective treatment there is** — provided child and parent are both motivated.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Alarms are the best first-line option:** they work well long term and relapse less often than medication does.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tell families an alarm can take 6-8 weeks to work.** It is usually advised from 6-7 years, depending on the child's physical ability, maturity and motivation.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Where to get one:** hire from some pharmacies, community continence services, tertiary centres or private practitioners; the Continence Foundation of Australia lists providers.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Mild to moderate intellectual impairment is no bar to alarm treatment;** for a child with hearing impairment, consider a vibrating alarm.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use an alarm if the carer** is struggling emotionally, is angry with or blaming the child, or is unlikely to manage the extra load of the alarm and the broken sleep it brings to the household.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The child owns the alarm** and at first may need waking to switch it off themselves. Success depends on the child being properly awake while getting up and going to the toilet.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Reward the actions, not dry nights:** rewards can help for waking up, or for getting to the toilet, once the alarm sounds.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Timeline:** early response by 4 weeks → keep going until 2 weeks of unbroken dry nights · no early response within 4 weeks → stop · still not fully dry at 3 months → rethink whether to continue, or try the alarm again in 3-6 months.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Overlearning, after 2 weeks or more of dryness:** have the child drink extra fluid in the hour before bed. The harder challenge over-conditions the bladder and may cut relapse.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tricyclics are no longer recommended:** they work less well than other treatments and carry more risk of adverse events.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Desmopressin is for** children in whom an alarm has failed or is unsuitable, or when quick, short-term improvement is the goal.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Most children relapse when desmopressin stops** (60-70 percent).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Desmopressin doses, over 6 years, at bedtime:** sublingual melt — start 120 micrograms, and if needed raise after 1-2 weeks to at most 240 micrograms; oral tablet — start 200 micrograms, and if needed raise to 400 micrograms.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use the intranasal route:** it carries a higher risk of hyponatraemia.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Limit fluids from 1 hour before each dose to at least 8 hours after it.** A child who cannot keep to the fluid limit must not have desmopressin.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Review at 4 weeks and stop if there is no response. Every 3 months, stop for at least 1 week** to see whether wetting returns and the medicine is still needed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Lifting a sleeping child to the toilet, or waking and walking them there, does not lead to lasting dryness.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Parent-led waking, scheduled or random, only helps in the short term.** A young person who wakes themselves (a phone alarm or alarm clock) may find it a useful strategy.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider a general paediatrician or continence service for:** wetting that persists after a failed alarm; daytime or combined day and night wetting once UTI and constipation are excluded or treated; recurrent UTIs; comorbidities such as type 1 diabetes or physical or neurological problems; major psychological or behavioural problems (with mental health, paediatric or child protection referral if the concern is significant).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Enuresis — Bed wetting and Monosymptomatic Enuresis', last updated July 2019, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Enuresis_-_Bed_wetting_and_Monosymptomatic_Enuresis/, retrieved 2026-09-24
